blocks.text: Newton's second law of motion states that when a force acts on a body, it produces acceleration in the same direction. A force acting on a moving body along the direction of its velocity will change magnitude of the velocity (speed) keeping the direction unchanged. On the other hand, a constant force acting perpendicular to the velocity of a body moving in a circular path will change the direction but magnitude of velocity (speed) will remain the same. Such force makes the body move in a circle by producing a radial (or centripetal) acceleration and is called centripetal force (Centre seeking) force. Figure 3.6(a) shows a ball tied at the end of a string is whirled in a horizontal surface. It would not continue in a circular path if the string is snapped. Careful observation shows at once that if the string snaps, when the ball is at the point A, in Fig. 3.6 (b), the ball will follow the straight line path AB which is tangent AB at point A.

blocks.alt: A person stands below a horizontal shaded disc that marks the plane of the circle. His raised hand holds a string at the centre; the string runs to a ball on the edge of the circle. An arrow on the string, labelled F, points from the ball towards the hand.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.6(a): A ball tied to a string and whirled in a horizontal circle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.6(a)).

blocks.alt: A circle with centre O and an arrow on it showing anticlockwise motion. From the point A on the circle a line runs to O with an arrow F pointing towards O. A dashed arrow from A along the tangent ends at B.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.6(b): If the string snaps at A, the ball moves along the tangent AB (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.6(b)).

blocks.text: Thus, a force is needed to change the direction of velocity or motion of a body continuously at each point in circular motion moving with uniform speed. The force that does not alter speed but only direction at each point is a perpendicular force which acts along the radius of the circular path. This force always pulls the object towards the centre of the circular path. Its direction is perpendicular to the tangential velocity at each point.

blocks.alt: Points spaced round a circle, each with a velocity arrow v along the tangent; the arrows all have the same length but point in different directions as the body goes round clockwise. At one point the next velocity arrow is copied to the same tail, a dashed curve showing the move, and the short arrow joining the two tips, pointing towards the inside of the circle, is labelled delta v.
blocks.caption: Do You Know (PDF page 59): direction of motion changes continuously in circular motion (original drawing after the textbook's figure in this box).

blocks.text: The force needed to bend the straight path of the particle into a circular path is called the centripetal force.

blocks.title: Example 3.2
blocks.problem: If a CD spins at 210 rpm, what is the radial acceleration of a point on the outer rim of the CD? The CD is 12 cm in diameter.
steps: We convert 210 rpm into a frequency in revolutions per second (Hz).
Thus f = 210 rev/min × 1/60 min/s = 3.5 rev/s = 3.5 Hz
For each revolution, the CD rotates through an angle of 2π radians. The angular velocity is:
ω = 2πf = 2π rev/min × 3.5 min/s = 7.0 π rad s⁻¹
a = ω²r = (7.0π rad s⁻¹)² × 0.06 m = 29 m s⁻²

blocks.text: The units in the angular-velocity line are printed as 2π rev/min × 3.5 min/s. Each revolution is 2π rad and f = 3.5 rev/s, so it should read ω = 2πf = 2π rad/rev × 3.5 rev/s = 7.0π rad s⁻¹. The result is unchanged.

blocks.text: Curved flight at high speed requires a large centripetal force that makes the stunt dangerous even if the air planes are not so close.
blocks.title: Do You Know?
Example 3.3
blocks.problem: A ball tied to the end of a string, is swung in a vertical circle of radius r under the action of gravity as shown in Fig. 3.7. What will be the tension in the string when the ball is at the point A of the path and its speed is v at this point?
steps: For the ball to travel in a circle, the force acting on the ball must provide the required centripetal force. In this case, at point A, two forces act on the ball, the pull of the string and the weight w of the ball. These forces act along the radius at A, and so their vector sum must furnish the required centripetal force. We, therefore, have
T + w = mv²/r     as w = mg, therefore,
blocks.answer: If v²/r = g, then T will be zero and the centripetal force is just equal to the weight.

blocks.alt: A vertical circle with centre O and the top point A. At A an orange arrow v points to the left along the tangent, and two downward arrows lie along AO: a shorter blue one, w, and a longer green one, T. An arrow on the circle shows the ball going anticlockwise.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.7: A ball whirled in a vertical circle: at the top point A, the tension T and weight w both act along AO (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.7).

blocks.text: In every circular or orbital motion, centripetal force is needed which is provided by some agency.

items: When a ball is whirled in a horizontal circle with the help of a string, then tension in the string provides necessary centripetal force.
For an object placed on a turntable, the friction is the centripetal force.
The gravitational force is the cause of the Earth orbiting around the Sun, Moon and artificial satellites revolving around the Earth.
A normal or perpendicular magnetic force compels a charge particle moving along a straight path into a circular path.

When a vehicle takes turn on a road, it also needs centripetal force which is provided by the friction between the tyres and the road. If the road is slippery, then at high speed, the friction may not be sufficient enough to provided necessary centripetal force. Hence, vehicle will not be able to take turn and may skid or may even be toppled. To overcome this difficulty, the highway road is banked on turns. That is, the outer edge of the track is kept slightly higher than that of the inner edge.

blocks.text: Banked tracks are needed for turns that are taken so quickly that friction alone cannot provide energy for centripetal force.
blocks.title: Tid-bits

blocks.text: Friction does not provide energy here: it provides the centripetal force itself. The sentence should read: friction alone cannot provide the necessary centripetal force.
blocks.title: Book correction

blocks.text: We know that an object moves in a circle because of centripetal force. If the magnitude of applied force falls short of required centripetal force then the object will move away from the centre of the circle. The centrifuge (Fig. 3.8-a) functions on this basic principle.

Centrifuge: It is one of the most useful laboratory device. It helps to separate out denser and lighter particles from a mixture. The mixture is rotated at high speed for a specific time. In a laboratory setup, sample tubes are used where the denser particles will settle at the bottom and lighter particles will rise to the top of the sample tubes (Fig. 3.8-b).

blocks.alt: A vertical shaft carries a hub and two horizontal arms. A holder at the end of each arm grips a sample tube lying outwards, its closed rounded end pointing away from the shaft. A curved arrow round the shaft shows the rotation.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.8(b): Sample tubes of a centrifuge, whose denser particles settle at the bottom (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.8(b)).

blocks.text: The dryer of the washing machine also functions on the principle of centrifuge. The dryer consists of a long cylinder with hundreds of small holes on its wall. Wet clothes are piled up in this cylinder, which is then rotated rapidly about its axis. Water moves outward to the walls of the cylinder and thus, drained out through the holes. In this way, clothes become dry quickly.

Cream separator is another practical device which is used to separate cream form the milk. In this machine, milk is whirled rapidly. Since milk is a mixture of light and heavy particles, when it is rotated, the light particles gather near the axis of rotation whereas the heavy particles will go outwards and hence, cream can easily be separated from milk.
